lead: This unit follows the machine tool from punched tape to the CNC controller, and then to two processes that cut metal without a sharp edge. After it you can read and write a simple G-code part program, explain open-loop and closed-loop feed drives and interpolation, and compute the main numbers for EDM and abrasive water jet machining.
about: The unit starts with how punched-tape NC became stored-program CNC and shop-floor DNC (6.1), then opens up a turning centre and a machining centre: structure, guideways, spindle and feed drives (6.2). Chapter 6.3 explains the controller inside, covering point-to-point and contouring control, open and closed loops, interpolation, and the encoders, gratings and laser interferometer that measure axis position. Chapter 6.4 builds a part program by hand in G and M codes, and 6.5 shows how CAM software produces the same program through CL data and a post-processor. The last two chapters leave the cutting tool behind: 6.6 erodes metal with sparks in a dielectric, and 6.7 cuts it with a high-pressure abrasive water jet.

chapters.idea: Numerical control moved the instruction from a punched tape into a computer memory, and DNC moved it from the machine to a central computer.
chapters.depth: NC block diagram: tape reader, machine control unit (MCU), axis drives. Hard-wired logic versus stored program. What CNC adds on top: memory, editing at the machine, canned cycles, tool and cutter compensation, diagnostics, graphics. DNC and its three links: behind the tape reader (BTR), behind the MCU, and a special machine control; then distributed DNC over a shop network. Advantages and limits of each generation. Some syllabi use DNC for the old 'direct numerical control' link and for the newer 'distributed numerical control'; say which one you mean.

figure.title: Four generations of program storage
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain of four blocks showing punched-tape NC, stored-program CNC, a central DNC computer and networked CNC machines.

chapters.example: An NC part program has 4,200 characters in 70 blocks. The tape reader reads 300 characters per second and each block takes 25 s of machining. Find the reading time per block and the percentage of time the reader is idle. Characters per block = 4200 ÷ 70 = 60. Reading time = 60 ÷ 300 = 0.2 s. Idle time = 25 − 0.2 = 24.8 s, so idle percentage = 24.8 ÷ 25 × 100 = 99.2 %. The tape reader, not the cutter, decides how the machine is used.
chapters.trap: Calling CNC 'NC with a computer' and forgetting the stored program and editing. Also mixing DNC with open-loop control: DNC is about where the program lives, open loop is about whether the axis is measured.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 for the lathe and milling machine axes and motions.
chapters.leave: Open-loop and closed-loop axis control to 6.3, G-code syntax to 6.4, CAM to 6.5.

chapters.idea: A CNC machine is a stiff structure, low-friction guideways, a spindle drive and a feed drive, all sized to hold position under cutting force.
chapters.depth: Classification: turning centre (2-axis X and Z, slant bed, turret, tailstock, live tooling with C-axis), machining centre (vertical and horizontal, 3 to 5 axis, automatic tool changer, pallet changer), plus CNC drilling and grinding machines. Machine building: bed and column stiffness, damping, thermal symmetry, welded versus cast bases. Guideways: friction types (dovetail, box) and anti-friction types (linear bearing, hydrostatic); stick-slip. Ball screw and its lead, preload and backlash. Spindle drives: DC shunt motor and its speed control, AC spindle with vector drive, gear ranges. Feed drives: stepper motor in open loop, DC and AC servo motors with closed loop, torque, inertia and matching the drive to the load. Axis naming conventions.

figure.aria: A tree classifying CNC machine tools into turning centres, machining centres and other single-purpose CNC machines, with examples under each branch.

chapters.example: A stepper motor drives a ball screw of lead 5 mm per revolution. Step angle is 1.8° and the drive sends 2,000 pulses per second. Find the resolution and the feed rate. Steps per revolution = 360 ÷ 1.8 = 200. Resolution = 5 ÷ 200 = 0.025 mm per step. Feed rate = 2000 × 0.025 = 50 mm/s = 50 × 60 = 3000 mm/min.
chapters.trap: Using screw pitch and screw lead as if they were the same number, and forgetting that a stepper runs open loop while a servo motor is closed loop by an encoder.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for what the program does, Unit 5 for cutting force and spindle speed.
chapters.leave: Interpolation and control loops to 6.3, part programming to 6.4, encoders and gratings to 6.3.

chapters.idea: The controller turns a wanted path into a stream of axis position commands, and compares each command with the measured position.
chapters.depth: Controller hardware: CPU, program memory, PLC for machine logic (coolant, tool change, door), servo interface, operator panel. Types of control system: point-to-point, straight-cut and contouring (continuous path). Open loop and closed loop; position, velocity and current loops. Interpolators: reference-pulse (incremental) and reference-word (absolute, sampled); linear, circular and DDA interpolation; chord error from a small resolution. Axis measuring: incremental and absolute encoders, quadrature giving four counts per line, linear gratings, resolvers, and the laser interferometer used to calibrate and check positioning accuracy. Computer-aided inspection: touch probe in the spindle, coordinate measuring machine, in-process gauging.

figure.title: Closed-loop contouring control
figure.aria: A vertical flow from part program through interpolator and comparator to servo amplifier and slide, with a dashed feedback path from the encoder back to the comparator.

chapters.example: A line is interpolated from (0, 0) to (60, 40) mm. The resolution (basic length unit) is 0.01 mm and the feed rate is 1200 mm/min. Find the path length, the machining time and the pulse rate on each axis. Path length = √(60² + 40²) = √5200 = 72.11 mm. Time = 72.11 ÷ 1200 = 0.0601 min = 3.61 s. X pulses = 60 ÷ 0.01 = 6000, so X rate = 6000 ÷ 3.61 = 1662 pulses/s. Y pulses = 40 ÷ 0.01 = 4000, so Y rate = 4000 ÷ 3.61 = 1108 pulses/s.
chapters.trap: Treating open loop as 'no program feedback' instead of 'no axis measurement', and forgetting that a quadrature encoder gives four counts per grating line.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for drives and guideways, 6.1 for the program store.
chapters.leave: Block-by-block G-code syntax to 6.4, CAM to 6.5, the full metrology of CMMs to a metrology course.

chapters.idea: A part program is a list of blocks, and each block says where to go, how fast, and with what spindle.
chapters.depth: Word-address block format and the order of words; modal and non-modal codes; the safe start block. G codes: G00, G01, G02, G03, G90 and G91, work offsets G54 to G59, cutter radius compensation G41 and G42, tool length compensation G43, canned cycles G81, G83 and G84, turning cycles G71 and G70. M codes for spindle and program end, F in mm/min for milling and mm/rev for turning, S and T words. Absolute versus incremental programming, cutter radius compensation and the offset path it creates. Writing a simple milling program and a simple turning program, with a sketch of the tool path.

figure.aria: A directed rectangle of four tool-path points A, B, C and D, each edge labelled with the G-code move that joins them, clockwise from the start point A.

chapters.example: A rectangular contour 80 mm by 50 mm is milled with a 10 mm diameter cutter at 150 mm/min. With G41 the tool centre runs on an offset path of 90 mm by 60 mm. Offset path length = 2 × (90 + 60) = 300 mm, so time = 300 ÷ 150 = 2.00 min. Without compensation the tool centre follows 2 × (80 + 50) = 260 mm at 1.73 min, but the part comes out 10 mm undersize on each side. Program: N10 G21 G90 G54; N20 T01 M06; N30 S1200 M03; N40 G00 X-10 Y-10 Z5; N50 G01 Z-3 F50; N60 G41 D01 X0 Y0 F150; N70 Y50; N80 X80; N90 Y0; N100 X0; N110 G40 X-10 Y-10; N120 G00 Z50; N130 M05; N140 M30.
chapters.trap: Mixing G90 and G91 in the same pass, and getting G02 versus G03 wrong: the direction is judged looking down the +Z axis towards the work, clockwise being G02.
chapters.prereq: 6.3 for interpolation and work offsets, Unit 5 for cutting speed and feed.
chapters.leave: Post-processors and CL data to 6.5, probing and inspection to 6.3.

chapters.idea: CAM software turns a CAD model into machine-independent CL data, and a post-processor turns CL data into G code for one machine.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at this point, so keep it short. Geometry statements and motion statements of an APT-like language; CL data as the neutral cutter-location output; the post-processor and why one CL file can serve several machines; roughing and finishing strategies, stepover and stepdown, lead-in and lead-out; simulation and collision checking; feature-based programming. The point to carry away is the split between tool path and machine code.

figure.title: From model to machine
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain from CAD model to CAM tool path in CL data, then a post-processor, a G-code file and the CNC machine.

chapters.example: A circular pocket of diameter 100 mm is milled with a 20 mm cutter at 8 mm stepover and 200 mm/min feed. Find the number of rings and the cutting time. Pocket radius = 50 mm, cutter radius = 10 mm, so the tool centre may reach 40 mm. Rings at radii 8, 16, 24, 32 and 40 mm: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 rings. Total path length = 2π × (8 + 16 + 24 + 32 + 40) = 2π × 120 = 754.0 mm. Time = 754.0 ÷ 200 = 3.77 min, plus entry and retract moves.
chapters.trap: Believing CAM writes machine code directly. CL data is neutral; without the correct post-processor the program will not run on a given control.
chapters.prereq: 6.4 for the block format the post-processor must produce.
chapters.leave: Stereolithography, FDM, SLS and rapid tooling are listed inside this unit in some syllabi; they are taught in Unit 7, not repeated here.

chapters.idea: EDM removes metal by repeated electric sparks across a dielectric-filled gap, so there is no cutting force and the tool never touches the work.
chapters.depth: Principle of spark erosion: pulse generator, tool electrode as cathode, workpiece as anode, dielectric fluid that insulates, ionises and flushes debris. Servo control of the gap and why a fixed feed fails. Pulse parameters: on-time, off-time, duty cycle, peak current, gap voltage. Electrode materials (graphite, copper, brass wire) and electrode wear. Die-sinking and wire EDM; flushing methods. Effect of parameters on material removal rate, surface finish, overcut and recast layer. Workpiece must conduct. Advantages, limitations and typical applications such as dies, moulds and hard alloys.

figure.title: Energy path in a die-sinking EDM
figure.aria: A block diagram in which a pulse generator and a servo head act on the tool electrode, a spark crosses the gap in dielectric to erode the workpiece, and dielectric flow clears the gap.

chapters.example: An EDM run uses gap voltage 25 V, peak current 20 A, pulse on-time 100 µs and off-time 100 µs. Find the energy per spark, the pulse frequency, the duty cycle and the average power. Energy per spark = 25 × 20 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.05 J. Period = 100 + 100 = 200 µs, so frequency = 1 ÷ 200 × 10⁻⁶ = 5000 sparks per second. Duty cycle = 100 ÷ 200 = 0.5, that is 50 %. Average power = 0.05 × 5000 = 250 W, which also equals 25 × 20 × 0.5.
chapters.trap: Thinking EDM cuts any material: the work must conduct electricity. Also confusing wire EDM, where a travelling wire is the electrode, with die-sinking, where a shaped electrode is sunk into the work.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for servo feed drives, basic electrical ideas of voltage, current and energy.
chapters.leave: Laser and electron beam machining to a later unit or course; surface integrity measurements to metrology.

chapters.idea: Abrasive water jet machining cuts by eroding the work with a very fast jet of water carrying abrasive particles.
chapters.depth: Water jet alone for soft materials, abrasive water jet for metals, glass, stone and composites. Pressure generation: pump and intensifier, accumulator to smooth the pulses, pressures of a few hundred MPa. Orifice that forms the jet, mixing tube where abrasive is entrained, standoff distance, traverse rate, kerf width and taper, abrasive type and size such as garnet. Effect of pressure, abrasive flow rate, standoff and traverse speed on depth of cut and finish. No heat affected zone, small cutting force, narrow kerf. Advantages, limitations, applications, and a short comparison with laser cutting.

figure.title: Water and abrasive path to the cut
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow from high-pressure pump and intensifier through the orifice and mixing tube, where abrasive joins, to the workpiece being cut.

chapters.example: Water at 300 MPa enters the orifice at 4 L/min. Take water density as 1000 kg/m³. Find the jet velocity and the hydraulic power. Velocity = √(2P ÷ ρ) = √(2 × 300 × 10⁶ ÷ 1000) = √600000 = 774.6 m/s. Flow = 4 L/min = 4 ÷ 1000 ÷ 60 = 6.67 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s. Power = P × flow = 300 × 10⁶ × 6.67 × 10⁻⁵ = 20 000 W = 20 kW.
chapters.trap: Putting the abrasive through the pump. Abrasive is entrained after the orifice, in the mixing tube, so it never passes the high-pressure seals. Also watch units: 300 MPa is 3000 bar, not 300 bar.
chapters.prereq: Basic fluid mechanics, especially Bernoulli's equation and continuity; Unit 5 for surface finish comparison.
chapters.leave: Laser and plasma cutting to Unit 4 (laser welding) or a later course; abrasive particle mechanics beyond the energy balance to a postgraduate course.
